Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/slate

# Slate

Slate is a film studio any agent can run. Every stage of a film is a `slate` command, every check is a gate, and
everything a film knows lives in its own folder, so any agent in any session can pick up exactly where the last one
stopped. This skill is the front door: it routes the request, runs intake, keeps the goal whole and hands each stage to
its craft skill.

Two words used throughout:
- **The owner** is the person Slate works for. They approve spend, the two sittings, the look, and anything published.
- **The requester** is whoever asked for this film: often the owner, sometimes someone they work with, sometimes an
  autonomous agent working for them.

## 1. Route the request before you run anything

| The request | What you do |
|---|---|
| **Open**: "make a video", "a short video of a paper boat in a storm", no length, format or brand named ("short" isn't a length), and no lane picked | Ask exactly one question, alone in its message: *"Do you want a full production or a quick generated clip?"* Run nothing and write nothing until they answer. Brand, length and format come after. |
| **Scoped**: a length, a format, a brand or a destination is named ("a 45-second launch video for …", "a 15-second 9:16 reel for …'s spring sale, captions burned in") | Straight to production (section 3). Don't ask the lane question. |
| **The quick clip, picked** (at your question, or up front: "a quick generated clip, not a full production") and no brand involved | The fast lane: hand over to Higgsfield's own skills (higgsfield-generate for a clip, higgsfield-video-explainer for a narrated explainer). No `slate new`. Mind the credits (below). |
| **Brand work**, even when it asks for "a quick Higgsfield clip" | Never the fast lane. It's a Slate production (a short express film suits it), and any generated shot runs through `slate gen` on the Cloud API: estimated, ledgered and judged against the brand's references. Say why in one line. |
| **Recording an app** to check its UI, transitions or motion (screen recordings, frame-by-frame QA, jank, flicker) | Not Slate: use video-verifier. Its web path goes through Aside, never another browser. |
| **Not a film**: web work that mentions video (a `<video>` tag, a hero video's CSS), an email, a single image | Not Slate. Do the task as the ordinary job it is. |
| **Post or publish a film** | Only a file the owner approved: its SHA-256 matches their approval and the delivery manifest marks it approved for publishing. Otherwise say which approval is missing, and stop. Slate never posts anything itself. |
| **Live action to shoot, or audio description** | Out of scope in this version. Say so, and offer what Slate can make instead. |

**Credits.** Higgsfield's skills stay installed globally because the owner uses them directly, but outside Slate they
generate on Higgsfield's app credits, a separate pool from the Cloud API balance, and that pool isn't funded by
default. If the fast lane stops for credits, say so plainly and offer a Slate production instead. Inside Slate every
generation runs on the Cloud API. Details and edge cases: [routing](references/routing.md).

## 2. Every working session starts the same way

1. **`slate status` first.** In a film folder (or with `--film <id>`) it lists every stage as fresh, stale, missing,
   locked or skipped, the sittings, open questions, locks and the one next command. Outside a film it lists the films
   on this machine. Trust it over your memory and over any summary.
2. **Snapshot the balances**, with one label for the whole session: `slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>`.
   At the end, run the same `slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>` again, then
   `slate ledger reconcile --session <label>`, so spend made through the chat connectors is caught. Slate can't read
   Higgsfield's balance itself: if a Higgsfield connector or its skills ran in the session, record that balance at
   both ends too, `slate ledger snapshot --provider higgsfield --balance <n> --session <label>`, with the number from
   the connector or the dashboard.
3. **Read `brief/GOAL.md` and `brief/PRODUCTION.md`.** After any summary or compaction, re-derive the checklist from the
   verbatim request in GOAL.md, never from memory, and assume something was lost until you've checked.
4. **Do the next thing** `slate status` names, with the skill for that stage (section 4).

## 3. Starting a film: intake

Goal fidelity comes first. The dropped requirement is never the headline; it's the aside, the "and also", the second
message.

1. **Capture every ask** in the requester's own words: split on every "and", list, comma and follow-up. Vague asks
   become intent items rather than disappearing. Restate the list back if anything is ambiguous.
2. **Check the brand**: `slate brand validate <brand>`.
   - No pack for the brand: onboarding comes first, before any script (`slate brand init <brand>`, then the
     slate-brand skill). A film looks right only when its look is built from the brand's own design system and a
     motion law measured from reference films; generic looks were rejected four times on the first film.
   - A pack whose four references (truth, look and motion, voice, sound) aren't all approved: finish onboarding with
     `slate brand onboard <brand>` before the script. The neutral `demo` pack is the exception: it exists for trials,
     tests and demos, and its look test rides in the film's pre-production sitting.
   - Autonomous films refuse any brand without all four references approved.
3. **Choose the format** from Slate's templates (reel, ad, explainer, brand film and the rest: [formats](references/formats.md);
   each is a JSON file in Slate's `formats/` folder, named for the format). The format sets runtime, aspect, pace,
   structure, loudness, captions and safe zones.
4. **Settle mode, generation and budget** ([modes](references/modes.md), [budgets](references/budgets.md)): supervised
   unless the requester says otherwise; generation `rarely` unless they ask for more or none.
5. **Make the film**, with the request verbatim:
   ```
   slate new <film-id> --brand <brand> --format <format> --request "<the request, word for word>" --source "<who asked>"
   ```
   Add `--mode`, `--generation`, `--runtime` or `--aspect` when the brief sets them; `--request-file` takes a long
   request from a file. This writes film.json (clock, size, budget, mode), `brief/GOAL.md` (the request and a checklist
   of every ask) and `brief/PRODUCTION.md`, and starts the film's git history.
6. **Record later messages** the same way, verbatim. GOAL.md names the commands that add a message and mark an ask
   done; done always needs evidence.
7. **Go as far as asked.** When the requester says how far to take it ("as far as the script"), stop there and end by
   naming the next step in so many words: for a supervised film it's the pre-production sitting, where the owner
   approves the checklist, the claims, the script and the look before anything is voiced or rendered.

Intake in depth: [intake](references/intake.md).

## 4. The production, stage by stage

| # | Stage | Skill | Commands | Who approves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Brand onboarding (once per brand) | slate-brand | `slate brand init`, `slate brand onboard`, `slate analyze`, `slate brand approve` | the owner approves four references |
| 1 | Brief | slate (this) | `slate new` | pre-production sitting |
| 2 | Truth: sources, claims, sample data | slate-story | `brief/truth.json`, `slate script build` | pre-production sitting (claims) |
| 3 | Treatment and script | slate-story | `script/script.json`, `slate script build` | pre-production sitting |
| 4 | Voice: cast or design, then every line | slate-voice | `slate voice cast`, `slate voice design`, `slate voice tts` | shortlist at the sitting |
| 5 | Timing | slate-story | `slate timing` | none: frame-exact or nothing is written |
| 6 | Look test (skipped when the brand's look is approved) | slate-motion, slate-brand | `slate render` of a short test | pre-production sitting |
| 7 | Kit, builders' brief, acts, captures | slate-build | `slate emit-events`, `slate check`, `slate capture ios` | hero moments, in the packet |
| 8 | Generated shots (only where allowed) | slate-generate | `slate plates plan`, `slate gen run` | takes, in the packet |
| 9 | Score, sound and mix | slate-sound | `slate score plan`, `slate mix`, `slate verify` | sound proofs, in the packet |
| 10 | Render with true motion blur | slate-finish | `slate render` | none: gates |
| 11 | Master | slate-finish | `slate master --ae` (supervised, on the owner's go) or `slate master --ffmpeg` | the owner starts the AE finish |
| 12 | Validate and deliver | slate-qa, slate-finish | `slate qa`, `slate deliver` | final-cut sitting |
| 13 | Review and correct | slate-finish, slate-qa | `slate review`, the same gates again | the owner's notes |

`slate make <target>` rebuilds only what's stale, in order. The method behind the table, with every machine gate, is in
[orchestration](references/orchestration.md); the stages are one clock, so a re-voice re-times everything downstream.

**Parallel work.** If you can run sub-agents, build acts in parallel, one builder per act under one brief; otherwise
build them in order. Either way a builder owns only its act's files, gets a first working version of every shot onto
disk fast, and keeps its NOTES.md current (slate-build).

## 5. Sittings, packets and approvals

- **Two sittings block a supervised film.** The pre-production sitting approves the checklist, the claims, the script,
  the voice shortlist and the look test. The final-cut sitting approves the film. Stop and hand over at each one:
  finish the packet, say plainly what's waiting for them, and don't start the next stage.
- **Packets don't block.** Hero moments, generated takes and sound proofs arrive in review packets the owner answers
  when they like; keep working on everything that doesn't depend on them.
- **An approval is bound to exact bytes.** Record each one with the command `slate status` names for it: it stores
  the SHA-256 of what was approved, so a changed file is no longer approved. Approved takes, score takes, plates and the
  final cut are locked by hash and never regenerated without an explicit force and a spend approval.
- **Only a person approves.** Never record an approval on anyone's behalf, never read approval into silence, and never
  treat a REVIEW verdict as a pass. Voices, sound and looks are picked by ear and eye; your measurements only shortlist.
- **Asking for a decision:** name it in one line, then ask a few concrete sub-questions whose answers settle it (their
  situation, their preference in practice, the edge case). If your agent has an interactive question tool, use it.
  Then say which way the answers point, and read free-text answers literally.

More: [approvals](references/approvals.md).

## 6. Budgets and spend

- Every paid call goes through Slate's ledger: estimate, budget check, an in-flight row with its request id, then the
  result. `slate budget show` has the month and each film's budget; `slate ledger list` has every paid call.
- A film's budget is a hard stop. 1.5 times is allowed only for marked rework. Spending past it needs the owner's
  recorded yes, and an autonomous film can never raise its own.
- **Slate never buys credits, upgrades a plan or starts a licence.** When a balance runs out, the work stops and asks.
- An optional extra that costs real credits (a dedicated score swell is about 1,100 to 1,500) is offered with its price
  and made only on the owner's yes, even when the budget would cover it.
- Replay is the default for tests and demos (`SLATE_FAKE_VENDORS=1`); `--live` spends for real.

Default budgets by format: [budgets](references/budgets.md).

## 7. Modes

- **Supervised** (the default): both sittings block; spend past the film's budget asks first; After Effects finishes
  it on the owner's go.
- **Express**: a short film runs straight to a review cut, and every approval is batched into the final-cut sitting.
- **Draft**: no generated plates, a library voice, fewer motion-blur samples. For animatics and quick variants. Never
  delivered as final.
- **Autonomous** (agents working for the owner): approved brands and approved claims only, every generation waits for
  the owner's yes, no After Effects, a separate reviewer grades the cut before it parks, and every output stays "not
  approved for publishing" until the owner approves that exact file.

The full rules: [modes](references/modes.md).

## 8. The tracker

`brief/GOAL.md` holds the request verbatim and the checklist of every ask; `brief/PRODUCTION.md` holds the asks,
every direction change (numbered and quoted exactly), open questions, revisions, approvals and the status table. Slate
keeps the blocks between its markers current; write anything else around them. Status words mean one thing each:
**done** is verified with named evidence; a proof is not a finished shot. `slate status --write` refreshes the table.
See [tracker](references/tracker.md).

## 9. Perfect, don't replace

When the owner approves something and adds notes, the notes are perfecting notes. Apply them to that exact artifact,
keep everything else as it was, and check the revision against the approved version by measurement (levels against
the voice, sync, palette). A note that seems to need a new approach gets a question first. Research only fixes a named
flaw; it never becomes a redesign. (One film's sound went off the rails exactly this way: small notes were answered
with a new sound system, and the effects that had stood out ended up buried.) `slate revise start <file> --notes …
--by <name>` turns the notes into a checklist of changes to that file, `slate revise check` measures the revision
against the approved version, and `slate revise done` refuses to close while anything else moved.
See [review and correct](references/review-and-correct.md).

## 10. Resilience

A production can run for days and outlive every agent that works on it.
- Everything a film knows is in its folder; `slate status` tells any agent where it stands.
- Long work (renders, masters, word timings, score composition, generation batches) runs as detached jobs in the
  queue: `--detach` returns a job id at once; follow it with `slate job status <id>`, `slate job wait <id>` and
  `slate job log <id>`. A dying agent, a sleeping Mac or a rate limit doesn't lose it: a job turned away by a vendor's
  rate limit (exit 75) goes back in the queue and tries again after the vendor's own wait.
- **Nothing prompts.** Research slices are killed after ten minutes with stdin as a pipe, so never start anything that
  waits for input. Keys are typed by a person in their own Terminal with `slate connect`, never in chat.
- **Inside the OpenClaw gateway, every paid stage is a job.** The gateway's egress proxy blocks the vendors, and the
  job runner works outside it: run voicing, music and generation with `--detach` or `slate job submit`, never inline
  ([agents and connectors](references/agents-and-connectors.md)).
- Save early and often: a session can end without warning.

See [resilience](references/resilience.md).

## 11. Protections

- **Voices:** designed or library voices by default; the owner's own voice only as a professional clone they verified
  themselves; anyone else's only as a real recording, never a clone, and never a public figure's.
- **People and claims:** no invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real, and no claim without a source.
- **AI labels:** none unless the law requires one. Slate still records which voices and shots are synthetic, internally,
  and platform rules on realistic AI voices or people are the owner's call per platform.
- **Company material:** company source code is read in place and never copied; brand material goes to a generator only
  when the brand owner allows it.
- **Spend:** never buy, never upgrade, never call a vendor's tool that uploads a user's skills or profile.
- **Browsers:** never open a web browser. Read the web with fetch and search tools; any page that must be driven goes
  through Aside.

The why behind each: [protections](references/protections.md).

## 12. Helpers, vendor skills, licences

- **Optional helpers:** ponder as a QA loop over every shot; visionary for hero moments; goal-fidelity for the
  checklist; asset-creator (vector drawing), canvas-design (frames), frontend-design (component looks) and
  avoid-ai-writing (script polish). None is required; Slate works without them.
- **Vendor skills:** Remotion's and ElevenLabs' skills live inside Slate's engine folder, not globally, and Slate's
  rules override theirs where they disagree. Higgsfield's stay global. Slate never deletes a vendor skill; if one keeps
  winning a request Slate should get, adjust Slate's own trigger with the owner's one-time permission.
- **Code you never copy:** OpenMontage is AGPL, and copying its code would force that licence on Slate. Ideas only.
  Licences in depth: [licences](references/licences.md).

## Reference files

- [routing](references/routing.md): every routing case, the one question, the fast lane and its credits.
- [intake](references/intake.md): capturing the brief, re-deriving the checklist, the brand check.
- [formats](references/formats.md): the format templates and derived films.
- [modes](references/modes.md): supervised, express, draft and autonomous, rule by rule.
- [approvals](references/approvals.md): sittings, packets, what counts as approval, asking for decisions.
- [budgets](references/budgets.md): default budgets, the ledger, never buying.
- [tracker](references/tracker.md): GOAL.md, PRODUCTION.md, status words, direction changes.
- [orchestration](references/orchestration.md): the method as a workflow, parallel builders, production routes.
- [review-and-correct](references/review-and-correct.md): review packets, notes, targeted fixes, versions.
- [resilience](references/resilience.md): detached jobs, sessions that end, files agents read.
- [protections](references/protections.md): voices, claims, labels, company material, spend, browsers.
- [agents-and-connectors](references/agents-and-connectors.md): the agents, the CLI, MCP, the chat lane.
- [dependencies](references/dependencies.md): tools, vendor skills, optional helpers, checking a tool first.
- [licences](references/licences.md): Remotion, Adobe, Eleven Music, ElevenLabs plans, AGPL code, fonts, sounds.
- [research](references/research.md): reading vendor docs, dated sources, the web without a browser.

`slate guide <topic>` prints these same files for an agent that can't read the skill folder.

Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/goal-fidelity

# Goal fidelity

The failure this exists to kill: on a big, multi-part request, do part of it, then
lose track of a feature that was explicitly asked for — and only "discover" the
miss when the user points it out. "Oh, you're right, I missed that" is the exact
outcome this skill prevents. Delivering 80% of a goal and calling it done is a
failure, not a partial success.

## The loop

### 1. Decompose — extract EVERY requirement, before doing anything

Re-read the request slowly and pull out each distinct ask into an explicit list.
The dropped requirement is almost never the headline — it's the one in an aside, a
subordinate clause, or a "and also…" at the end. Hunt those specifically:

- Split on every "and", "also", "plus", "oh and", numbered/bulleted item, and
  comma-separated clause.
- Capture implied deliverables (e.g. "make it public with good docs" = repo +
  public visibility + README + docs — four items, not one).
- Capture soft/vague asks as intent items ("make it feel less clunky") rather than
  dropping them because they're not crisp.
- Include earlier open threads the user hasn't closed (a question they asked that
  you haven't answered yet).

Write the list where it stays visible: the **Task tools** (`TaskCreate`) for
substantial work; an inline checklist in your reply for smaller asks. Restate the
full set back to the user so they can catch anything you misread.

### 2. Execute — one item at a time, checklist stays authoritative

Work the items. Mark one done **only when it's actually verified**, not when you've
written the code / started it. Depth on the current thread must not evict the other
threads from memory — the visible list is what holds them.

### 3. Verify — the completion gate (do this before you say "done")

Before finishing, **re-read the user's ORIGINAL words** — not your summary, not the
checklist alone. Walk each requirement and ask: is this genuinely delivered and
verified, or did I drift/skip/half-do it? Anything partial or untouched means the
task is NOT complete — keep going. This gate is mandatory for multi-part work.

### 4. Report — result against each item

State the outcome per requirement (done / how verified / or explicitly "not done
because X"). This makes any gap visible to the user instead of buried.

## Surviving context loss

Long sessions get summarized/compacted, and **summaries drop sub-requirements**.
So: after any compaction, or whenever a task has run long, **re-derive the
checklist from the original request** and diff it against what you've actually
delivered. Assume something was lost and go find it. If the original request has
scrolled out of reach, ask the user to restate the goal rather than guessing.

## Honest omission

If a requirement genuinely can't be met (blocked, needs a decision, out of scope),
**say so explicitly and prominently** — surface it as an open item. A stated
blocker is fine. A silent omission is the failure this skill exists to prevent.

## Anti-patterns

- Starting to code before enumerating the full ask.
- Treating the first/biggest item as "the task" and the rest as optional.
- Marking things done from intent instead of verification.
- Ending on "I've done the main pieces" while a named feature sits untouched.
- Trusting a summary's requirement list over the user's original message.

=================== intake.md
# Intake: the brief, in the requester's own words

Intake turns a request into a film folder with the goal written down exactly as it was asked. Everything later is
checked against that record, so it has to be complete and verbatim.

## 1. Capture every ask

Big requests get half-delivered when one ask quietly drops out. It's almost never the headline; it's the aside, the
subordinate clause, the "oh, and also" at the end, the second message an hour later.

- Split the request on every "and", "also", "plus", list item and comma-separated clause.
- Write implied deliverables out: "a reel with captions for Instagram and TikTok" is a reel, burned-in captions, and
  two platforms' safe zones.
- Keep vague asks as intent items ("make it feel less corporate") instead of dropping them because they aren't crisp.
- Carry open threads: a question the requester asked that nobody has answered yet is an ask too.
- If anything is ambiguous, restate the list back so they can correct it.

## 2. Write it down verbatim

```
slate new <film-id> --brand <brand> --format <format> --request "<the request, word for word>" --source "<who asked>"
```

- `--request` takes the words exactly as they arrived, typos included. `--request-file <path>` reads a long one.
- `brief/GOAL.md` then holds the request, a checklist row per ask (auto-split rows are flagged for you to check) and the
  settings rows (format, brand, budget, mode). `brief/PRODUCTION.md` is the live tracker (see tracker.md).
- Every later message that adds or changes an ask goes in verbatim too, with who sent it. GOAL.md names the command.
- If the original request was cut off or summarized away, say so in the tracker, and mark any ask you rebuilt from
  follow-ups as reconstructed.

**After any summary or compaction, re-derive the checklist from the verbatim request, never from memory.** Summaries
drop sub-requirements; assume something was lost and go find it.

## 3. Check the brand

`slate brand validate <brand>` reports the pack and which of its four references are approved.

| What you find | What happens |
|---|---|
| No pack for this brand | Onboarding first (`slate brand init <brand>`, then slate-brand). No script before it. |
| A pack with references still unapproved | Finish onboarding (`slate brand onboard <brand>`) before the script. |
| The neutral `demo` pack | Go ahead: it's for trials, tests and demos; its look test rides in the film's pre-production sitting. |
| All four ref
[… 12,874 characters left out of the recording …]
ence is made locally. |

For scale: a code-only film spends nothing on generation; a hybrid film with about 40 seconds of generated plates, a
few takes each, spent roughly $8 to 30; an all-generated six-minute cut would be roughly $55 to 95.

## Spend Slate can't see

Generations made in a chat through the hosted connectors (Higgsfield's or ElevenLabs') bypass the ledger. The ledger
catches them by comparing balance snapshots:

```
slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>        # at the start of a working session
slate ledger snapshot --all --session <label>        # at the end, with the same label
slate ledger reconcile --session <label>
```

`--all` records every balance Slate can read by itself (ElevenLabs'); it skips Higgsfield, which has no balance
endpoint. When a Higgsfield connector or Higgsfield's own skills ran in the session, record its balance at both ends
from the connector's balance tool or the dashboard:

```
slate ledger snapshot --provider higgsfield --balance <n> --session <label>
```

A reconcile that finds unexplained spend is REVIEW, for the owner to look at. A provider with only one snapshot in the
session is UNCHECKED, never a pass.

## Two wallets at Higgsfield

The **Cloud API** balance pays for every Slate generation and is the one funded lane. **App credits** pay for
Higgsfield's CLI, app and hosted connector, including its own skills; that pool isn't funded by default, so the fast
lane may stop for credits. Neither is ever topped up by an agent.

Cloud API credit expires a year after it's bought; app-plan credits expire every billing cycle. When the owner buys
Cloud API credit, it's for the films actually planned, never ahead of them.

## Watching spend during a film

- `slate ledger list --film <id>` has every paid call for the film; `slate ledger inflight` shows calls still waiting.
- Before a batch (a full voicing, a score, several takes), say what it will cost and what's left of the budget.
- An optional extra that costs real credits (a dedicated score swell is about 1,100 to 1,500 credits) is offered with
  its price and made only on the owner's yes, even when the budget would cover it.
- Before spending past an approval (a recomposition, a re-voice of approved lines), try what's on hand first: an unused
  take often measures better than a new one, and costs nothing.

# Approvals: sittings, packets and the owner's yes

People judge what machines can't: the look, the voice, the sound, the hero moments and the final cut. Slate's job is to
put the right thing in front of them at the right time, record their decision against the exact bytes they judged, and
never mistake anything else for a yes.

## The two sittings (they block)

| Sitting | What it approves | What you prepare |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-production** | the checklist of asks, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist, and the look test when the brand's look isn't approved yet | GOAL.md with every ask; the truth pack and the claims list; SCRIPT.md; a casting reel (slate-voice); a moving 10 to 15 second look test with sound (slate-motion) |
| **Final cut** | the film itself (in express mode, everything above too) | the review packet (`slate review`): the phone cut, the contact sheet, what changed, open questions; every gate's status |

At a sitting: finish the packet, say plainly what's waiting for them and why, and stop. Don't start the next stage
"to save time"; it will be rebuilt if they change their mind.

## Packets (they don't block)

Hero moments, generated takes, sound proofs, voice takes and score takes go into review packets the owner answers when
they like. Keep working on everything that doesn't depend on them. When they answer, record it.

## What an approval is

- **Bound to exact bytes.** Record each approval with the command `slate status` names for that stage. It stores the
  SHA-256 of the file approved, who approved it and their words. Change the file and it's no longer approved.
- **Kinds Slate records:** checklist, claims, script, voice shortlist, look test, final cut (the sittings); hero,
  plate, sound proof, take, score take (packets); and spend (a yes to spend again on something already paid for).
- **Locks follow.** Approved takes, score takes, plates and the final cut are locked by content hash. Regenerating one
  needs an explicit force and a recorded spend approval.
- **Only a person approves.** Never record an approval on someone's behalf, never read approval into silence or a
  thumbs-up on something else, and never treat a REVIEW gate as a pass.
- **By ear and by eye.** Voices, sound and looks are chosen by the owner listening and watching. Measurements shortlist
  and catch faults; they never decide.

Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/slate-story

# slate-story

The story is data. One hand-edited file, `script/script.json`, holds every act and shot: what the voice says, what's on
screen, what the picture does, and where every claim comes from. `slate script build` checks it through the script
gates and writes the storyboard and a readable SCRIPT.md, and it refuses to write anything while a gate fails. Nothing
downstream is typed by hand: shot lengths, timecodes and frames all come from this file and the voice's real reads.

This skill covers stages 2 (truth), 3 (treatment and script) and 5 (timing) of the production. The front door (the
slate skill) has already made the film folder and the brief.

## 1. Truth first

Before a line is written, know what's true and who says so.
- The **brand's truth** (from onboarding): its claim authority, sources, approved claims, never-claim list, banned
  words and sample data.
- The **film's truth pack**, `brief/truth.json`: the sources this film relies on, each pinned (a commit, a retrieval
  date or a hash), the researched claims that cite them, what this film never claims, and its sample data.
- The product's own code, read in place at a pinned commit, is the only product truth: it wins over docs, demos,
  prototypes and older films. The owner's rulings win over the code for what's claimed.

Every claim and every number said or shown must be on the brand's approved list or cite a pinned source. Autonomous
films use approved claims only. Research method and templates: [truth](references/truth.md). The rules every frame and
line obeys: [truth packs](references/truth-packs.md).

## 2. The treatment

For anything longer than a short ad, write a treatment before the script: the idea as a reframe, why this runtime, act
by act, the emotional arc, one signature moment per act, the voice and the look and the sound in a line each, what the
film never shows, and the owner's calls so far. Keep it to a page or two. Template and craft:
[treatment](references/treatment.md); story shapes that work: [structure](references/structure.md).

## 3. The script as data

Write `script/script.json`: acts of shots, each with an id, the VO line, the on-screen words, the picture, the
transition out, and its sources and claims. Shape, fields and a worked example: [script as data](references/script-as-data.md).

```
slate script build --check      # the gates only; writes nothing
slate script build              # gates, then script/storyboard.json and script/SCRIPT.md
```

The gates: schema, structure, pace (2.6 words a second or less, per shot), read time, on-screen density, runtime
(within 10% of the target), banned words (VO, on screen and picture), claims, numbers, quotes (no invented testimonial),
sources, and the shot-id freeze. A failure lists what to fix; fix the script, never the generated files.
`storyboard.json` and `SCRIPT.md` say "generated: do not edit by hand".

Shot ids freeze when the build passes; once scenes use them, a renumber is refused. Add shots with new ids instead.

## 4. Writing the voice-over

- **Pace:** at most 2.6 words a second, per shot. Plan shot lengths from the words, then let the real reads re-time
  them (section 6).
- **Read time:** every on-screen statement holds, once fully built, at least max(1.5 s, 0.4 s + 0.3 s per word);
  numbers hold 2 s after they land.
- **Density:** at most 12 on-screen words per shot; on-screen text is keywords (about 40% of what the voice says or
  less), never a transcript of the VO.
- **Numbers and symbols** are written the way they're spoken or shown consistently; the clock knows how "664" or "&" is
  said, so word lookups find them.
- **Brand words** go in the brand's lexicon, so the voice checks can hear them said in full.
- **The words are final before voicing.** Direction (tone, pauses) is added later as audio tags that never change a
  word (slate-voice).

More craft, with the fixes for each gate: [VO writing](references/vo-writing.md).

## 5. The visionary bar

Make beautiful things that would make someone cry. Every act gets **one signature moment**: the beat people remember,
built inside the brand's own visual language (no glows, flares, particles or bounce). A correct but ordinary animation
doesn't meet the bar. If the visionary skill is available, use it before designing any hero moment: reframe, go wide
across lenses, kill the median, push one idea to a signature. Mark each act's moment in the treatment and in the script
(the shot's `notes`), so builders know where the film's weight is. See [signature moments](references/signature-moments.md).

## 6. After voicing: the clock

Once the takes are approved (slate-voice):
```
slate script build --from-takes     # every voiced shot re-timed from its approved take
slate timing                        # shots, voice cues, word timings, events, timeline on the film's clock
```
- `slate timing` writes `timing/shots.json`, `vo_cues.json`, `vo_words.json`, `events.json` and `timeline.json`. It
  refuses to write unless the frames are exact and contiguous.
- Word timings come from Whisper by default; a word lookup never throws, it falls back to an estimate and records a
  miss. The miss list must be empty before any act is handed in (slate-build).
- Once an act render is registered the timing locks; only the owner can decide to re-time, with a reason.

## 7. Handing over to the pre-production sitting

When the script builds clean (and the treatment, the truth pack and the voice shortlist are ready), stop. The
pre-production sitting approves the checklist, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist and, when the brand's look
isn't approved, the look test. Say what's ready, where it is (SCRIPT.md, the truth pack, the casting reel), and what
each decision is. Record the owner's calls on the draft (trims, keeps, confirmations) as numbered decisions in the
tracker, with their words.

## Rules that hold everywhere

- One hand-edited source. Never edit storyboard.json, SCRIPT.md or the timing files; change script.json and rebuild.
- Nothing is invented: every UI element, word and number maps to a citation (truth packs).
- No invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real; quotes carry who said them and a pinned source.
- Runtime stays within 10% of the target unless the requester asks otherwise or you justify it in the tracker.
- The picture can be restaged freely by builders; the words, beats and timing are the script's.

## References

- [truth](references/truth.md): researching truth; pinned sources; product-truth and capability-brief templates.
- [truth-packs](references/truth-packs.md): the rules every line and frame obeys about claims, data and the product.
- [treatment](references/treatment.md): the treatment template and how to write each part.
- [structure](references/structure.md): story shapes that work: bookends, payoffs, journeys, the end card.
- [script-as-data](references/script-as-data.md): script.json field by field, a worked example, the gates and fixes.
- [vo-writing](references/vo-writing.md): pace, read time, density, numbers, brand words, a character's own words.
- [signature-moments](references/signature-moments.md): the visionary bar and one signature moment per act.

A truth pack is the brand's truth (from onboarding) plus the film's (`brief/truth.json`). The script gates, the claims

claims just as the voice can.

## Nothing invented

- Every UI element, word and number on screen maps to a citation. Never show UI the product doesn't have.

- Product names follow the product's current code, not older materials.

# Truth research: sources you can pin and cite

A film is only as trustworthy as the sources behind it. Truth research finds what's actually true about the product
and the brand, pins each source so it can be re-checked, and records who rules on what's claimed.

## The order of authority

1. **The owner's rulings** on what's claimed. A feature can exist in the code and still be ruled out for the film
   ("that's not true" means it doesn't appear).
2. **The product's code**, read in place at a pinned commit and cited `path:line`. It wins over everything below.
3. **The brand's website, live product pages, public demos and guidelines**, read and cited with the date.
4. **Docs, prototypes, demos and older films**: layout references only. They drift: names change, numbers move,
   features are retired. When they disagree with the code, the code wins; when a product demo's wording disagrees with
   the product's code, the code wins.

For a brand the owner doesn't own, the brand's **claim authority** (a named person there) rules on claims and brand use.

**Nothing is invented**: every UI element, word and number in the film maps to a citation in the truth pack. A concept
screen (something not built) needs the requester's explicit sign-off and a visible "concept" treatment. The rules that
follow from this are in [truth packs](truth-packs.md).

## Pinning a source

Every source in `brief/truth.json` has an id and a pin: a commit, a retrieval date or a SHA-256. A claim cites a pinned
source by id, with where in it (`path:line`, a page, a section). A number with no pinned source doesn't go in the film.

```json
}
```

- Read it in place, on the machine that holds it, with read-only commands (`git show`, `git grep` at the pinned

- Quote the exact copy the produc

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/visionary

# Visionary

Quinn invokes this when the safe, correct, median answer is a failure. The goal is
work that makes someone stop — a feature, a look, an interaction, an experience
that "no ordinary person or typical AI would think of." Ordinary AI brainstorming
loses because it returns the *center of the distribution*: the ten things anyone
would list. Visionary means deliberately leaving that center.

**The bar (hold everything to it):** would this make Quinn say *"I've never seen
that"* — and want to build it tonight? Three tests every surviving idea must pass:
1. **Visceral** — a first-glance gut hit; you feel it before you analyze it.
2. **Non-obvious** — a typical person/AI would not have produced it; it required a
   reframe, an analogy, or an inversion to reach.
3. **Real** — specific enough to build or draw, with the insight that makes it
   special nameable in one sentence. A vague "AI-powered X" is not an idea.

Anchor taste to Quinn's north star — **The Browser Company (Arc/Dia)**: craft,
warmth, personality, physical/springy motion — the *feeling*, expressed inside the
project's own tokens, never by copying a brand. (See `~/.claude/memory/` design
notes and the relevant taste skill: `frontend-design`, `[company]-frontend-taste`,
`swiftui-taste`.)

## The method

### 0. Reframe before you ideate

The biggest visionary move is usually solving a *better problem*, not solving the
stated one more cleverly. Before generating:
- State the request as a job-to-be-done, then ask **"what's the real problem
  behind this?"** and **"what would make this problem not need solving at all?"**
- Challenge the premise. If the ask is a proposed solution ("add a settings
  page"), find the need underneath ("the user never has to configure this").
- Name the **10× version**, not the 10% one: what would this look like if it were
  the best in the world at what it does?

### 1. Diverge hard — generate through many lenses, not one

Quantity first, judgment later. Run the idea through deliberately different lenses;
each lens is blind to the others, which is what surfaces ideas a single train of
thought never reaches. Aim for volume, then cut.

- **First principles** — strip to physics/truth, rebuild without inherited
  assumptions. What's actually necessary here?
- **Cross-domain steal** — how is this solved in a *far* field (games, aviation,
  transit, nature, print, music, film, hardware)? Transplant the mechanism.
- **Invert the constraint** — take the thing everyone treats as fixed and remove
  or reverse it. What if it were instant / free / infinite / one-tap / had no UI?
- **What would a master do** — channel a specific visionary (Ive on reduction,
  TBC on warmth, Nintendo on delight, Bloomberg on density, Teenage Engineering on
  playful hardware). Not "be creative" — *be that person's taste* for one pass.
- **Emotional / experiential** — design the *feeling* first (calm? powerful?
  playful? proud?), then the artifact that produces it. What's the one moment a
  user would screenshot?
- **Future-back** — assume it's 5 years ahead and this is obvious in hindsight;
  describe that obvious-future version, then pull it to now.
- **Signature detail** — the tiny, obsessive thing that signals craft (a motion
  curve, a sound, a microcopy voice, a single perfect transition).

For a genuine hard brainstorm — and when workflow orchestration is available
(ultracode / the Workflow tool) — **fan these lenses out in parallel** (one agent
per lens, generating aggressively), then a **taste judge** pass that scores every
candidate on the three tests and keeps only the top few. Parallel divergent
generation + adversarial selection is how you beat median output; don't simulate a
panel in one voice when you can actually run one.

### 2. Kill the median

Explicitly discard every idea a normal list would contain. If an idea would appear
on the first page of a Google search for "ideas for X", cut it. What remains are
the candidates worth Quinn's time. Say what you're cutting and why, briefly — it
proves you left the center on purpose.

### 3. Converge with conviction — no porridge

Do **not** average three safe ideas into a mushy compromise. Pick the one (maybe
two) that hit hardest and commit. For each survivor:
- Name the **insight** in one sentence (the reframe/analogy/inversion that makes it
  work).
- Make it **concrete** — the feature spec, the layout, the interaction, the exact
  signature moment. Draw it, mock it, or spec it precisely.
- Note the **risk** honestly and how to de-risk it.

### 4. Push the winner to a signature

Take the chosen direction and design the one detail that sets it apart — the thing
people will remember and describe to a friend. This is where visionary earns its
name: not the concept alone, but the executed, distinctive moment. If it's UI,
render/mock it and judge it by eye against the taste north star (and grade it with
the local design model when relevant — see the `design-model-build` skill).

## Guardrails

- **Grounded, not unhinged.** Visionary ≠ impossible. Every idea must be buildable
  in this stack and honest about cost; wild framing, real substance.
- **Distinctive over derivative.** Channel the *feeling* of masters and brands;
  never clone their assets, names, or trade dress.
- **Serve the actual goal.** Novelty that doesn't make the product better is
  decoration. The reframe must still solve Quinn's real problem.
- **One signature per surface, not chaos.** A screen/product gets one nameable
  bold move executed precisely — not ten competing gimmicks.
- **Then hand back to rigor.** Once a direction is chosen, exit visionary mode and
  execute it completely (`goal-fidelity` — build every part, verify, don't drop
  the details). Vision without follow-through is the other way to fail.

| Token | Seconds | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **tick** | 0.18 | chip flips, checks, a dot lighting |
| **quick** | 0.3 | small UI elements, re-layouts |
| **base** | 0.5 | standard entrances: a line of type, a card |
| **broad** | 0.75 | panels, wipes, short count-ups |
| **camera** | 1.1 | camera moves and carried pieces |
| **signature** | 1.6 | the logo build and the act's one signature moment |

Seconds are the source of truth; frames come from each film's own rate.

**Exits** run 0.75× the duration of their entrance.

## Staggers

- **char**: 0.04 s
- **word**: 0.08 s
- **line**: 0.12 s
- **block**: 0.18 s
- **Cap:** a group's whole spread is at most 0.5 s; at most 50% of the group's own entrance; more than 8 items are grouped, never staggered one by one.

## Overshoot

None: nothing bounces, and nothing passes its target.
Nothing bounces. A container that grows uses settle, which lands without passing its target.

## Signature motion

- **name**: keystone build
- **what**: the mark builds tile by tile, left to right, and its clay keystone drops in last and lands
- **logo**: mark
- **ease**: arrive
- **duration**: signature
- **sound**: one hollow wood knock as the keystone lands, with a small felt note under it

## Rules

- Linear only for things that show time: progress, playhead, spin.
- Loops: min_period_s 0.8.
- Never scale anything from zero: entrances start from at least 85% of their size.
- Never bounce or overshoot: the studio's motion is calm; settle lands without passing its target.
- Never cut hard between shots: pieces are carried from beat to beat (exception: a cut hidden inside a fast move's blur).
- Never crossfade between shots: it double-exposes type into mud.
- Never use an editor's default ease: every visible move uses one of the named eases.

# Every film, checked: the treatment

Film `demo-new-feature-reel` · social reel · 15 s · 9:16 (1080×1920, 30 fps) · brand `demo` · supervised · draft-1, 2026-10-01.
The script is `script/script.json` (readable as `script/SCRIPT.md`); the claims are in `brief/truth.json`.

**Read this first.** The brief asks for a reel announcing Demo Studio's new feature, but the demo pack names no new
feature. Rather than invent one, draft-1 announces the pack's one approved capability, *every film is checked before it
ships* (claim demo-2), as that feature. Whether that's the feature meant, whether the film may call it new, and whether
it has a name are question q1, which parks the film until the owner answers.

## 1. The idea, as a reframe

A check is invisible work, so an announcement usually just says it happened. This reel shows it happening:
twenty-four checks become the studio's own mark, and the film leaves only when the last one lands. "Checked before it
ships" stops being a promise about a process and becomes the moment something can stand on its own, like an arch once
its keystone is set.

## 2. Why 15 seconds

The brief asks for 15 seconds, and the idea fits it. One idea (every film is checked before it ships), one carrier (the
checks), one signature moment (the keystone). Seventeen words of voice leave the middle three seconds wordless for the
landing. Shorter loses the held beat; longer pads a single idea. Planned at the format's speech rate, it runs 15.0 s
against the 15 s target (±10% allowed). The real reads re-time it after voicing.

## 3. Act by act

One act, four beats: hook, idea, payoff, end.

| Beat | Shot | The viewer learns | The viewer feels | It hands on by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hook | S01 | Demo Studio has something new | curious | the film card stays; empty check slots arrive under it |
| Idea | S02 | every film is checked before it ships: 24 checks (sample data) | reassured | the filled rows lift off the card |
| Payoff | S03 | the last check is what lets a film leave | a held breath, then release | the mark holds where it landed |
| End | S04 | the studio's name, and the feature in three words | settled | (the film ends on the card) |

## 4. The emotional arc

| Shot | Starts | Ends |
|---|---|---|
| S01 | scrolling, idle | curious: what's new? |
| S02 | curious | reassured: nothing leaves unchecked |
| S03 | reassured | moved: the stillness, then the landing |
| S04 | moved | settled: Demo Studio, every film checked |

## 5. The signature moment (S03)

The film's one keystone build. The three rows of eight checks condense into the mark's three tiles in its own build
order (top left, top right, bottom left). The keystone's cell waits empty for one still beat. Then the clay keystone
drops in from above and lands, with one hollow wood knock and the felt marimba's D, F sharp and A rising under it. The
build guides strike away and the film card lifts out of frame: checked, it ships. The mark stands alone.

**The insight:** until its keystone is set, an arch can't stand without the frame that holds it up. The last check is
the keystone.

**Why it meets the bar:** the brand's own objects do something unexpected and true. The sample checks literally become
the mark: 24 is the brand's stagger group of eight times the mark's three tiles. There's no glow, flare, particle or
bounce, nothing else moves, the sound lands with it, and no words compete with it.

**Cut as median in the visionary pass:** ticks appearing one by one as the moment itself, a progress bar to 100%, an
approval stamp or badge (a stamp reads as an endorsement), a magnifying glass, and any celebration effect.

## 6. Voice, look and sound

- **Voice:** the demo pack's library voice (George, ElevenLabs): warm and unhurried, a narrator who's sure rather than
  selling. Never hype, never a whisper. Casting comes next, and the shortlist goes to the sitting.
- **Look:** the demo pack's flat look. Warm stone page, a white card, ink ticks, Public Sans with tabular figures, and
  one clay thing per frame (the New chip, then the keystone). The demo's look test rides in the pre-production sitting.
- **Sound:** a soft pad in D major (84 to 96 BPM), three wood clicks for the three rows, silence under the held beat,
  then one hollow wood knock with the felt marimba motif on the landing. No chimes, bells or risers.

## 7. What the film never shows or says

- A name for the feature, because none is sourced (q1).
- A release date or availability, a price, or how the checks are made (by people or by software). None of it is
  sourced; "available now", "automatically" and "automated" are on the film's never-claim list.
- Customers, testimonials, or Demo Studio as a real company (the brand's never-claim list).
- An approval stamp, seal or badge, or any UI the studio doesn't have. The film card is abstract paper with no copy.
- A sample number without its sample-data label, or a sample number in the voice.
- The brand's banned words: guaranteed, revolutionary, best-in-class, world-class.

## 8. The owner's calls

None yet. Waiting on the owner:

1. **q1, the feature** (it parks the film): is it the checks, may the film call it new, and does it have a name?
2. **A call to action:** the end card has none, because Demo Studio has no site or product page to point to. Say if you
   want one, and where it should point.

## 9. Notes for builders

- One carrier: the 24 checks become the mark. The card is the film, and it leaves only after the keystone lands.
- Keep everything inside the safe column the three platforms share: clear of the top 15%, the bottom 35%, 11.1% on the
  left and 17.8% on the right. Captions are burned in above the bottom keep-out.
